title: Fill the chemical day tank to the mark and close the transfer valve
instruction: Top up the day tank: open the transfer valve, watch the level, and close the valve when the level reaches the red mark. Don't let it overflow.
context: Harm: a sodium hypochlorite day tank left filling runs over onto the floor, a chemical spill and a slip hazard. Safe finish: valve opened, level brought to the red mark, valve closed. Rule: Recommended Standards for Water Works (Ten States Standards, 2012 edition) 5.1.11 Day tanks, which requires a calibrated gauge showing the actual volume, and 5.1.9 Storage of chemicals, which requires a level indicator, an overflow and a basin or drain for accidental spills; Illinois's adoption, 35 Ill. Adm. Code 604.1105(l)(6), adds that filling a day tank must not be automated, so an operator attends the transfer. Done by: water and wastewater treatment plant and system operators.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left. Everything is taped down. Day tank: a white polyethylene open-topped box, 12 x 12 cm inside, 6 mm walls, 16 cm tall, centred at x 32, y -9, standing on a dark rubber mat 16 x 16 cm, 1 mm thick. Up its front face (towards the arms) runs a level strip of eight segments, each 10 cm wide, 1.6 cm tall and 4 mm thick, 2 mm apart, the lowest starting 1 cm above the table: dark when empty, blue when full, 100 mL per segment. The lowest two are lit at the start (200 mL, a quarter full). A red mark, 10 cm wide, 3 mm tall and 5 mm thick, sits on the strip at the top of the sixth segment (600 mL). Transfer valve: a brass block 5 x 5 x 5 cm (3 kg in the sim, so it stays put when pushed) centred at x 20, y -24, with a dark plastic handle 3 cm along x, 2 cm along y and 5 cm tall standing on its top. The handle slides 3 cm along y: at its stop towards the robot's left it is closed (the start); pushed 3 cm towards the robot's right it is open. On a real bench the strip is a graduated sight gauge on the tank and the valve is a sliding gate on the transfer line.
scoring: Scored from the end state, with the trial run to its limit, plus one latch: whether the level ever went above 800 mL (the rim), which on a real bench is liquid on the mat. The level is read in mL against the strip, 100 mL per segment. The valve is closed when the handle is within 30 percent of its travel (9 mm) of its closed stop; it passes liquid past 70 percent (21 mm), and while it does the level rises 50 mL/s. Level 500 to 650 mL and valve closed: 1.0. Level 500 to 650 mL with the handle not closed (anywhere past 9 mm): 0.3. Level 350 to 500 mL and valve closed (stopped early): 0.5. Level 650 to 800 mL and valve closed (overshot, no spill): 0.3. Level 350 to 500 mL or 650 to 800 mL with the handle not closed: 0.1. Overflowed at any time (above 800 mL, liquid on the mat): 0, whatever follows. Level under 350 mL, which includes never opening the valve (200 mL) and doing nothing: 0. Valve tipped more than 20 degrees from upright at the end: 0. Shoving the valve along the table changes nothing: the handle is read against the block. A person scores a real trial from a photo of the strip and of the handle against a tape measure at the end, and the video for an overflow.
reset_notes: Drain the tank back to 200 mL (two segments lit), dry the mat, and slide the handle back to its closed stop, towards the robot's left. Nothing is consumed. Run with -E object_jitter=0 (one fixed layout).
fidelity: Approximate. No liquid: the level is a count in Python that rises 50 mL/s while the handle is past 70 percent of its travel, shown by recolouring the strip's segments, 100 mL each, with no real liquid height. An overflow recolours the mat blue and latches. The valve is a sliding block on a damped prismatic joint with no spring, standing in for a gate valve on a transfer line; nothing flows through it. Tank, strip and mark are rigid fixed boxes. The valve is held by its 3 kg weight rather than tape. Rubber-like friction everywhere.
